title: Nothing Here Is Nailed
logline: In a palm-shaded working yard behind a south-coast beach, eight or nine separate pieces of timber that are useless on their own — a hollowed log, two raised side planks, shaped inner frames, two cross booms and a float — are drilled, stitched and lashed together with coir cord and no iron at all, and every binding is drawn up and tested before the finished hull is put in water that will test all of them at once.
human_question: What holds a set of separate, ordinary parts together well enough to carry someone across?

place.what_kind_of_place: A working stretch of the island's south coast where the sea is close on one side and a shallow lagoon lies a few hundred metres behind, and where the ground between them is coconut, sand, low walls and palm-thatch. The boats of this coast are pulled up on the sand in rows, bows to the sea. The yard itself is small: hard-packed sand under palms, a thatched or tin lean-to, a hull on blocks with wedges under it, a second hull turned over beside it, and a scatter of parts that do not yet belong to anything — a hollowed log with its ends still square, two long side planks, curved inner frames waiting to be fitted, two straight cross booms, and a shaped float lying on its own in the shade. The tools are few and almost all of them are hand tools: an adze, a chisel, a mallet, a hand drill or a heated iron for burning holes, a wooden needle, a caulking iron, a bucket, and hanks of coir cord. There is no iron in the boat at any point. The one power tool is likely to be a planer, and it changes nothing about the joints. Around the yard, this being a working coast, there are engines being mended, fibreglass hulls being rubbed down, and craft of every generation lying within a hundred metres of each other.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because the concept is physically true in this yard and nowhere else on the slate: a thing that carries a person across water is assembled from parts that are individually useless, and the whole of it is held by bindings that can be seen, counted and tested. Wide and from height, this coast is one of the most graphic in the country: a white break, a line of drawn-up hulls with their floats sticking out at right angles like a row of insects, palms, and behind them a flat lagoon that goes to mirror in the last hour of the day, so that the same hull can be filmed from above as a shape made of separate sticks and then as one object moving on still water. Close, the film is small exact operations in a fixed order: holes drilled or burned in pairs along an edge, a strip of matting laid in the seam, cord passed through with a wooden needle and pulled tight with a foot braced against the plank, a cross-stitch built up along a metre of hull, frames set and lashed, booms bound down at four points each, and the float lashed on last with its own kind of turn. And the film has one action that decides everything: each binding is hauled up, struck, leaned on and looked at, and the ones that are not right are cut off and done again, because a single slack lashing does not make a boat look unsafe.
place.what_moves_or_changes: A pile becomes one object, and after that it is never tested one part at a time again. At the start the parts are not even related: a log that has been lying to season, planks cut months ago, a float that came from a different tree. They are fitted dry, marked, taken apart and fitted again. Once the stitching starts the hull stops being adjustable, because the holes are in it; once the frames are in, the shape is fixed; once the booms are down the boat has a width and a balance. The cord itself changes as it works: coir swells when wet, so a binding drawn up dry is not the same binding an hour after launch, and everything in the sequence assumes that. And the last change is the one nobody can stage: the hull goes into water, the float takes weight for the first time, and every binding is tested at once by something that does not care in which order they were made. Across a much longer clock, this kind of construction is going out. Plank-built and moulded hulls, engines and mooring in a harbour have replaced most of it, and what is left is largely repair.
place.when_it_looks_best: The dry, calm months on this coast, because the work is done in the open, the sand is workable, and a launch needs a beach that can be used rather than a shore break that cannot. Within a day, early morning for the yard, when the light comes through the palms in bars and the sand still holds the night's damp, and the last hour for the drawn-up boats and the lagoon behind them, when the water goes to mirror and a hull reads as one shape rather than as a set of parts. The middle of the day is worth filming for the opposite reason: glare flattens everything, the yard is at its plainest and the work goes on anyway. The one thing that has to be waited for rather than lit is the first time the hull is in water.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A film about a boat being put together out of separate pieces of wood and a lot of cord. A log on blocks under palms with its ends still square; planks and frames lying apart in the shade; holes made in pairs along an edge; matting laid into a seam; a wooden needle pushed through and a cross-stitch built up a metre at a time; a foot braced against a plank while a turn is hauled tight; frames set and bound; two booms lashed down at four points each; a float bound on last; a binding cut off and done again; the hull carried down the sand and floated for the first time, with somebody standing on the booms to see what happens. It has a complete shape with nothing said over it, and anyone who likes hand tools, joinery without metal, or the plain suspense of whether something will hold, has a whole piece here.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same assembly becomes the sources' own image for the eight path factors, which the text states in one sentence: a raft made by binding great logs together helps in crossing the ocean, and that is why these eight are called limbs. The word the tradition uses for a factor means a limb, a part of a thing, and the books are insistent that the thirty-seven names reduce to fourteen actual qualities, with one of them turning up in nine places and another in eight, and that in the full sense all of them arise bound to one mind at once, while in ordinary practice only one at a time is available. A yard where separate timbers become one hull, where the count of parts is small and honest, and where the whole thing is only ever tested together, carries all of that without a lecture. The voice never says the boat is a person or the sea is suffering. It says the source used a bound raft as its picture, that the picture is about composition rather than effort, and that the limit of the picture is stated in the source itself.

sequence.on_screen: First light, high above the beach. A row of hulls drawn up bow-first with floats sticking out sideways, palms behind them, a white break in front. Then down into the yard: a hollowed log on blocks, planks, frames, booms and a float all lying apart in the shade, none of them touching.
sequence.voice: Nothing in this yard is a boat yet. A log that has been lying a year, two planks, a set of curved frames, two straight poles and a shaped float that came off a different tree. Every one of them is useless on its own and none of them will be held to the others by a single piece of iron.

sequence.on_screen: Holes made in pairs along the edge of a side plank and along the hull below it. A strip of matting laid into the seam. A wooden needle pushed through, the cord following, and the first stitches drawn up with a foot braced against the plank.
sequence.voice: The text this film is built on gives its own picture for the eight factors of the path, and it is this one. A raft made by binding great logs together is what helps in crossing an ocean; so these eight are called limbs, parts of the means, and the crossing is what they are for [C076-P:L1413]. The other book says the word plainly: a limb means a part, and the parts here are parts of the means and nothing else [C076-M:L107].

sequence.on_screen: Frames set inside the hull and bound in. Then the two cross booms laid over and lashed down at four points each, the turns built up and hauled tight, the whole structure suddenly rigid. A hand testing each binding in turn, leaning, striking, watching.
sequence.voice: The same book describes five of these qualities as powers, and it is careful about how they work together. Each of them destroys what stands against it without overriding the strength of the others; they are named like commanders on a field, each one doing its own work, none of them crowding the rest out [C076-P:L1238]. Every lashing on this hull holds without stopping the next one from holding.

sequence.on_screen: A binding that is not right: cut off with a knife, the cord pulled out and dropped, the hole cleaned, and the whole turn built again from the beginning. Nothing about the boat looks different before and after.
sequence.voice: One slack binding does not make a boat look unsafe. That is the whole reason this is done in the open, in order, and checked, and it is why a list of thirty-seven is not a list of thirty-seven separate skills.

sequence.on_screen: The float lashed on last, out at arm's length on the ends of the booms, with its own kind of turn. Then the finished hull from directly above: one object made of sticks, casting a single shadow on the sand.
sequence.voice: The count itself is smaller than it sounds. Thirty-seven items by name; fourteen actual things underneath them [C076-P:L1445]; and of those, one single quality turns up in nine different places on the list and another in eight [C076-P:L1453]. The long list is a few capacities seen from different angles and given different jobs, exactly as a hull is a few kinds of turn used in different places.

sequence.on_screen: The hull carried down the sand on shoulders and floated for the first time. The float settling, taking weight, lifting. Somebody standing on a boom. Water already in the stitched seam and swelling the cord.
sequence.voice: The name the tradition gives the minds this is all for is explained by one word: what carries a person across and beyond [C016-P:L25]. Everything that was built dry in that yard is now being tested at the same moment by something that does not care in what order it was made.

sequence.on_screen: The lagoon behind the beach in the last hour, gone to mirror. The hull moving on it as one shape. Then the yard again, empty, with the offcuts and the spoiled cord in a heap.
sequence.voice: And the source states its own limit, so the film does not have to pretend. In the full sense all of these arise bound to one mind at once, in a single moment [C076-P:L1465]. In the ordinary graded work that comes before it, the same book says, only one of them is available at a time [C076-P:L1467]. So a boat is a good picture of things that only work bound together, and it is not a picture of that moment, and nothing on this water is it.

sequence.on_screen: Last light on the drawn-up row from height, floats out sideways, shadows long. Two or three of the hulls are plank-built and one is moulded plastic, lying in the same line.
sequence.voice: Two things this film is not saying. Nobody in that yard is being presented as having attained anything; what is on screen is joinery, and the sources are explicit that nothing visible verifies anything of this kind in anybody. And this is not a lament for a dying craft. Most of the work on this coast now is repair, the boats in this row come from four different generations of building, and the people who own them chose what they chose for reasons of their own.

concept_merge.why_together: C076 is the film and C016 is the one word it needs at the launch. C076's Pradeepika gives the source's own simile in a single sentence: a raft made by binding eight great logs together helps in crossing the ocean, and for that reason the eight path factors are called limbs and causes of the way to nibbāna [C076-P:L1413]. Margaya glosses the word itself, saying that a limb means a part, a part of the means by which defilements are destroyed, and that these eight arise bound together with one mind at once [C076-M:L107]. Pradeepika also describes the five powers as defeating what opposes them without overriding one another's strength, using commanders on a battlefield as its picture [C076-P:L1238]; it reduces the thirty-seven to fourteen realities [C076-P:L1445] and points out that one single quality occupies nine places on the list and another eight [C076-P:L1453]; and it states the limit that makes human analogies safe, that all of them are obtained together in the supramundane path mind [C076-P:L1465] while for a practitioner working through the mundane purifications only one at a time is available [C076-P:L1467], which Margaya repeats [C076-M:L113]. C016 supplies one sentence and no more: the name of these minds is explained as what carries one across and beyond the worlds of existence [C016-P:L25]. A hull assembled from separate timbers with no iron in it, whose bindings are tested one at a time on the sand and then all at once in the water, puts the simile, its arithmetic and its limit on screen together.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the claim is about composition rather than about effort, and that the failure of any one part is invisible until the whole thing is loaded. Said flat, thirty-seven requisites is a curriculum. Put on a yard where a few kinds of turn are used in different places on one hull, it becomes the source's own arithmetic: a long list of names over a short list of actual things, each doing its own job without crushing the others. The film also gets the concept's hardest clause honestly, because a boat can show parts that only work bound together and can also show, at the moment of launch, that the binding was made in sequence while the test is simultaneous, which is exactly the difference the source draws between the gradual stage and the path moment. This idea keeps the subject it was given. What has changed is where the camera stands: the film is the binding and the testing, not a portrait of a boatwright, and there is no interview, no named craftsman and no account of anybody's trade or income in it.

concept_links.why: The film is the source's bound-raft simile, its arithmetic and its stated limit, and nothing else from a very large concept. The simile is spoken once, at the moment the first stitches are drawn up, and it is given as the source's picture rather than the film's [C076-P:L1413], with Margaya's gloss that a limb means a part of the means [C076-M:L107]. The account of the five powers, each defeating what opposes it without overriding the strength of the others, is spoken over booms being lashed down and each binding being tested in turn [C076-P:L1238]. The reduction of thirty-seven names to fourteen realities, and the fact that one quality occupies nine places on the list and another eight, is spoken over the finished hull seen from above as one object made of repeated turns [C076-P:L1445; C076-P:L1453]. The closing movement carries the digest's sharpest limit in the source's own terms: all of them arise together in the path mind [C076-P:L1465], while in the graded work before it only one is available at a time [C076-P:L1467]. Every limit in the digest that bears on this film is honoured and the hardest one is on screen. Everyday teamwork metaphors are explicitly denied the status of the path moment, by the film's own voice, in the beat that follows the launch. The thirty-seven are not presented as a self-improvement checklist. Mindfulness is not offered as stress relief and the body contemplation, the hindrances, the loving-kindness counts, the cautionary monastic stories and the gravely ill elder are not used at all. Right livelihood is not turned into career advice and the craft in the yard is never offered as a better or more spiritual way to earn a living. Balance is not softened into a self-care slogan. No real person is presented as having attained anything, and the film says so out loud in its last beat.

One sentence from this concept is narrated and it is placed at the only moment that can carry it. The source's explanation of the name of these minds as what carries one across and beyond the worlds of existence is spoken as the hull is floated for the first time and the float takes weight [C016-P:L25]; the film uses it as an etymology and never as a claim that this boat, this water or this far shore stands for anything. The digest's flattest ruling is honoured: a breakthrough, an epiphany or a conversion experience is not what the source means, so the launch is filmed as a working test and never as a moment of transformation, and nobody standing on the booms is presented as having crossed anything. The stages are not used as labels for any person on screen, which is stated in the closing beat. The rebirth pathways, the lamp simile, the treasure-house story, the yoked oxen and the lists of defilements removed at each path are not used, and the gender-sensitive clause the digest flags for expert checking is not touched. Nibbāna is not illustrated: the far water, the last light and the lagoon are allowed to be water and light, and the voice does not point past them.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the tradition's own picture for the factors of its path is a raft of bound logs, that the point of the picture is composition rather than effort, that a long list of names sits over a short list of actual qualities each doing its own job without crowding out the others, and that the source itself says these only come together completely in a single moment, while in ordinary practice they are available one at a time. The boat is the source's analogy and the film says so; nobody in it is described as having attained anything and no claim is made about anyone's skill.
what_must_be_real: A commission or a repair that was going to happen anyway, on a craft that will actually be used. No construction is revived, commissioned, subsidised or restarted for the film; if this kind of building has stopped here and only repair survives, the film is a repair. Nothing is taken apart and redone for a second take, no binding is cut off for the camera, and no stage of the work is delayed or brought forward for the light. The launch is the launch, once. Nobody is asked to demonstrate anything, nobody is asked to work faster or slower, and no tool is exchanged for a more traditional-looking one. The yard's owner decides what is filmed under the roof. Nobody is named or followed as a character, nobody is interviewed about mastery or patience, and the trade's decline is not presented as a tragedy or its practitioners as survivors.
position_hint: middle to late in the group, and after at least one film that has already shown a thing taken apart: it is the group's clearest statement that what carries somebody is assembled rather than singular, and it works best once the viewer has watched the opposite operation. It is also the group's most physical film and can carry a quieter one on either side of it. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Turning the boatwright into the subject, so that a person's skill, calm or judgement becomes the thing being admired, which the group's floor forbids.
Letting the launch read as a moment of transformation or arrival rather than as a working test of joints.
Speaking the raft simile as a lecture over the images instead of once, plainly, as the source's own picture.
Romanticising a precarious livelihood, or filming the trade's decline as a lament.
Staging or subsidising a form of construction that is no longer done here, which would be a fabrication.
Letting the far water or the last light stand in for the unconditioned, which cannot be filmed.
Making the boat an allegory of a person, so that the hull becomes a life and the sea becomes suffering.
Filming a launch or sea trial in a way that adds risk for the people aboard, or asking for one in conditions they would not choose.
Putting the yard's earnings, debts, buyers or the owner's household on screen; there is no money in this film.
drop_if: No yard on this coast still builds or repairs with stitched and lashed joints for real use, so the work would exist only because the film asked for it.
The only available work is a demonstration piece for visitors rather than a craft that will be used.
A launch or first float cannot be filmed inside the window, so the film's one simultaneous test is missing.
The yard will not allow an unbroken sequence to be filmed in its own order and at its own speed.
The work can only be filmed by asking the builders to repeat or explain what they are doing.

connections.note: One film takes a thing apart so that it cannot come back; this one puts separate things together so that they hold. The group's two ground-level films about removal and composition.
The same far-shore language approached through what is made to carry people rather than through the carrying itself.

selection.reason: The source's own image for its path is physically true in this yard: many ordinary parts bound into one thing that is only ever tested together, with the binding visible, countable and checkable.

review.note: Rewritten into the footage-led shape on 2026-09-24. The subject is unchanged and did not need to change: many separate parts made into one thing that then holds is exactly what the requisites of enlightenment are, and the source supplies the picture itself. What has changed is where the camera stands. The previous version was written around a builder, an apprentice and a commissioning family, with the craft's survival as its stake; this version films the binding and the testing and nothing else, with no interview, no named craftsman, no apprentice being judged against a master and no account of anybody's income or reputation, because the group's floor is that no real person's skill or composure may read as an attainment. Both concept links were re-read from the digests and every citation re-tested against digest evidence line by line. Two citations in the previous text have been replaced after checking: the raft simile is at the line stated here, and the limit about the factors arising together is carried by the source's own two sentences about the path mind and about the graded work rather than by a single paraphrase. The closing movement states the limit out loud, which is what keeps a boat from being offered as a picture of the path moment, and the last beat refuses both the attainment reading and the dying-craft lament.

suggested_location.name: The small-craft yards on the beach and lagoon shore between Ahangama and Habaraduwa, east of Galle

also_known_as.name: oruwa
also_known_as.meaning: the single-outrigger canoe of the island's west and south coasts: a hollowed log raised with sewn side planks, carrying a float on two booms

also_known_as.name: kollǣ
also_known_as.meaning: reported usage for the float that runs parallel to the hull on the ends of the booms; the spelling and the local currency of the word have not been checked with anyone in the trade

also_known_as.name: stitched construction
also_known_as.meaning: joining timbers by drilling paired holes and sewing them with cord, with matting or fibre laid in the seam, instead of using nails, bolts or screws

suggested_location.region: Galle District, Southern Province: the stretch of coast east of the harbour town where a shallow lagoon lies a few hundred metres behind the beach, and boats are drawn up on the sand in front of the coconut land
suggested_location.why_here: Because the craft this film needs belongs to this coast and the geography gives the film both of its views in one place. The single-outrigger canoe of the island's west and south coasts is documented as being built without iron: a shallow hull carved from one log, raised with side planks fixed on shaped inserted frames and sewn to the hull with coir, the seam covered with coconut matting and stitched through drilled holes, the booms lashed to the hull and the float lashed to the booms, with hand-twisted coir used for all of it. That is the whole film, and it is a construction in which every joint is a binding that can be counted and tested. This particular stretch is chosen because the sea is on one side and a large shallow lagoon is a few hundred metres behind, which gives a hull that can be filmed from height as a set of sticks on the sand in the morning and as one shape on mirror-flat water in the evening; because the coast carries craft of several generations lying in the same row, so the film does not have to pretend that this is the only way boats are made here; and because the immediate neighbours on this coast in this project's slate are already taken, so the film sits in country that is not otherwise being used. There is no private grief in the subject and nobody has to be an example of anything.
what_to_film: The drawn-up row from height at first light and in the last half hour, so the floats stand out sideways and the hulls read as assemblies rather than objects.
The parts lying apart in the yard before anything is joined: the hollowed log on blocks, the planks, the frames, the booms and the float, each on its own.
Holes being made in pairs along an edge, matting laid into the seam, and the first stitches drawn up, filmed close and long from one fixed position.
A single metre of cross-stitch built up from beginning to end without a cut, because the repetition is the concept.
Frames set and bound, and the booms lashed down at four points each, with the hull becoming rigid inside one shot.
Each binding being tested by hand: hauled, struck, leaned on, looked at, and either accepted or cut off.
A lashing cut off and remade from the beginning, filmed plainly, since the boat looks the same before and after.
The float bound on last, out at arm's length on the ends of the booms.
The finished hull from directly overhead on the sand, casting one shadow, and then carried down and floated for the first time.
The lagoon in the last hour with the hull on it as a single shape, and the yard afterwards with the offcuts and spoiled cord in a heap.
suggested_location.access: By the coast road east of the harbour town and then on to the beach and the lanes behind it; the yards are private working ground in people's compounds or on beach land held by fishing families, so everything depends on the yard whose work this is agreeing, and on approaching them through the fisheries office, a boat owners' association or somebody they already deal with rather than cold. This is a visited coast, which cuts both ways: people are used to cameras and also tired of them, and a crew that turns up for a day will be treated as tourism. The practical hazards are ordinary: an adze, a heated iron for burning holes, a heavy hull on blocks, and a launch through surf. Flying over occupied beach land and over a working shore needs the agreement of the people whose boats and houses are in frame, whatever the general position is, and a lagoon behind the beach may sit under its own restrictions. The work stops for rain and a launch waits for a usable beach.
suggested_location.best_time: The calm, dry months on this coast, and within them a block of consecutive days rather than single visits, since the film is one assembly followed through. Early mornings for the yard and the last hour for the drawn-up boats and the lagoon; the middle of the day deliberately, for glare and for the plainness of the work going on in it. The launch cannot be scheduled against the light and has to be taken when it happens, so a second short visit is worth planning for.

images.caption: Outrigger canoes drawn up on a beach elsewhere on the island's south coast, in the neighbouring district. A picture of the type of craft the film is about, not of this stretch of coast, any yard or any of this work.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, and unverified on the ground. From the sources above: the single-outrigger canoe of this island is a regional craft of the west and south coasts, built of wood with all fastenings chosen to be of coconut coir rope; the hull is a shallow dugout carved from one log and raised with side planks fixed on shaped inserted frames and sewn to the hull; to join the washboards to the dugout, holes are drilled along the edges, the seam is covered with coconut matting and the pieces are sewn together with a cross-stitch, the builder literally threading a needle and assembling the craft stitch by stitch; hand-twisted coir is used to bind the float to its booms and the booms to the hull; and the lashing of the sprits to the main boom and the hull, the fastening of the float to the booms and the use of rope grommets for detachable parts are described as critical to the craft. A museum record of one such canoe confirms the same construction. None of this is specific to the stretch of coast named here. Three things the film depends on are therefore inferences about this particular place and are the first to check on the ground: that a yard here still builds or at least re-stitches and re-lashes such craft for real use rather than for display; that a whole assembly, or a substantial repair, could be followed through in one yard across consecutive days; and that a first float or launch could be filmed inside a window. The coordinates are the published position of a village on this stretch of coast and are a direction towards the country the film needs, not a survey: no yard, builder, owner, boat or household has been identified or approached, and no permission has been sought from anyone. No photograph of a yard, a stitched seam or any of this work on this coast was found on Wikimedia Commons; the one image is of the craft type, photographed on another part of the south coast.

unknowns: Whether stitched and lashed construction is still done anywhere on this stretch of coast for boats that will actually be used, or whether only repair survives.
Whether a whole assembly, or a substantial repair, can be followed through in one yard across consecutive days without the order or the timing being adjusted.
Whether a first float or a launch falls inside a filming window, since the film's one simultaneous test depends on it.
Whether the cord used now is hand-twisted coir, bought coir or a synthetic substitute, which changes what the close work actually shows.
Whether a yard will allow filming without being asked to demonstrate, explain or repeat anything.
Whether height can be obtained over this beach and the lagoon behind it, and what the people whose boats and houses are in frame want about that.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is proposed by Claude from desk research and is unverified. No scene or shot is decided here.
